source.title: Tool Mediation Alters Refusal Mechanisms in Large Language Models
source.authors: Abel Rodríguez; Giuseppe Garofalo; Lieven Desmet; Vera Rimmer

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes harm-related neuron contributions across conversational and tool-mediated channels, but does not test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common polysemantic neurons are, or whether they have coherent meanings.
record.gate_note: The neuron-level results concern contributions to harm representations across two renderings of the same intents. They do not measure the mixed-input responses, semantic coherence, or prevalence named by the claim versions. The study also discusses neuron localization, but does not use or test the polysemanticity claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures how late-MLP neurons contribute to a harm direction in conversational versus tool-mediated renderings of the same intents, and ablates channel-selective neuron sets. It never asks whether single neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how many neurons are polysemantic, or what causes polysemanticity. The word 'polysemantic' does not appear. Neuron localization work (Dai et al., Tang et al., Chen et al.) is cited only as a method. The record's 'discusses' overstates the link: the paper does not discuss polysemanticity at all.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors conclude that harm stays decodable under tool mediation, but its conversion into refusal differs: tool-mediated refusal has a higher effective threshold and partially distinct neuronal contributions. It is also more fragile under directional ablation and GCG. Much of the shift appears at tool exposure alone.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or apply the original polysemanticity methods; it studies refusal representations and neuron contributions in language models.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for polysemanticity measurements; the paper reports that channel-specific neuronal contributions are assessed using a shared harm direction and selected late-MLP layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-neuron late-MLP contributions to a shared harm direction are highly reproducible within a channel (ρ about 0.96–0.98) but agree much less across conversational and tool renderings (ρ 0.11–0.45). Ablating a channel's own selected neurons reduces its harm projection more than ablating the other channel's neurons or matched random ones, in all seven dense models. The PrivacyLens replication gives cross-channel ρ of 0.08–0.50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuronal contributions to a safety-relevant representation are context- or interface-specific within the same model, even for the same underlying intents.

record.problems: The study does not operationalize or measure polysemanticity, unrelated neuron inputs, semantic coherence, or the share of neurons with one versus multiple jobs. The reported neuron-profile correlations are specific to harm-related contributions across interaction channels.
record.rows_left_out: Neuron-ablation and attention-head results in Appendix C.6 are not included: they test causal contributions to channel-specific harm projections, not whether neurons have mixed or coherent meanings.

untested.parts: No measurement of neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and no prevalence by layer.
No manipulation of initialization, regularization or training noise.
No comparison of activation functions or architectures for polysemanticity. The dense vs MoE contrast concerns harm-contribution dissociation only.
No reinterpretation of apparently mixed neurons.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: The relation should be cites_only rather than discusses: polysemanticity is never mentioned, and neuron-level work is cited only as method. The gpt-oss-20b row's 'ceiling' appears to be taken from the cosine column (0.94) instead of the neuron-profile ceiling (0.72). The text also says within-channel ρ is 0.96–0.98, while the table shows 0.96–0.98 except gpt-oss.

versions.untested_parts: No vision models or image-classifier neurons are studied.
The study does not measure MLP neurons' responses to unrelated tokens or contexts, or the share of polysemantic neurons.
No test of superposition or capacity pressure as a cause of polysemanticity.
No test of initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures, or regularization for polysemanticity, and no such performance trade-off.
No investigation of whether apparently mixed neuron responses share a coherent feature or job.
No comparison of neuron explanations across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-channel Spearman correlation of per-neuron harm-contribution profiles using a shared harm direction.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation of neuron contribution profiles across channels; within-channel reproducibility ceiling also reported.
rows.note: The authors report lower agreement across channels than within channels; this measures channel-specific harm contributions, not polysemanticity.
rows.check: The measure is cross-channel rank agreement of per-neuron harm contributions, not mixed or unrelated neuron selectivity. The state 'observed' has no version to refer to and should be cannot_determine.
